stimulusMaterial.body:
ENGLISH PASSAGE 1: The Clock Above Alder Street
[1] After three months of fundraising [[a neighborhood restoration crew began]] to repair the brass clock above Alder Street Market. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a market hall built in 1911, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using a laser scan and a box of hand-labeled gears, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] wear marks showed that an earlier repairer had reversed two nearly identical wheels. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because replacement parts would have erased those clues. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the crew cleaned and reused the original wheels. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the clock kept accurate time through a week of rain. [[The most effective conclusion should emphasize that the repair preserved evidence of how local mechanics once solved problems.]]

[1] After several cloudy evenings [[a coastal ecology class began]] to count juvenile crabs in tide pools after sunset. Before beginning, the group listed what it already knew, what would need to be measured, and which decisions could still be reversed without damaging the project. [2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of a protected inlet beside the school, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using red lamps, quadrats, and waterproof tally sheets, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] the smallest crabs appeared most often under flat stones near eelgrass. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because bright white light changed the animals’ movement. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the class switched to dim red lamps and repeated the first survey. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, the second set of counts was more consistent. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because different observers used different abbreviations. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the students built a glossary before entering the remaining records. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, searches began returning complete groups of related observations. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] cloud cover explained several gaps that had once looked like missing pages. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because different observers used different abbreviations. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the students built a glossary before entering the remaining records. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner. [9] The writer is considering adding this sentence here: “Every tool was returned to a labeled drawer at the end of each session.” [10] Ultimately, searches began returning complete groups of related observations. stimulusMaterial.body:
READING PASSAGE 1: The Blue Ledger
When Mara inherited the repair shop, everyone asked whether she would keep the blue ledger. The question annoyed her because the ledger was neither rare nor beautiful. Its cloth cover had faded to the gray-blue of a rainy curb, and the pages smelled faintly of machine oil. Her uncle Tomas had recorded every repair in it: date, customer, object, fault, and charge. Beside many entries he had added a tiny sketch—a hinge, a spring, the tooth of a gear.

Mara preferred the tablet she carried from bench to bench. It could search part numbers, enlarge photographs, and total invoices without smudging her fingers. During her first week as owner, she placed the ledger in a cabinet and began a clean digital list. The shop seemed lighter with the old book out of sight.

Then a school custodian brought in a wall clock that lost exactly seven minutes each day. Mara cleaned the movement, tested the spring, and adjusted the pendulum. The clock still lost seven minutes. She searched manufacturers’ diagrams and repair forums, but the model number led only to photographs of clocks that looked similar. At closing time, almost as a joke, she opened the cabinet.

Tomas’s entry from nineteen years earlier described the same clock. His sketch showed a narrow washer behind the minute hand. “Not original,” he had written. “Owner wants face preserved; compensate at pendulum.” Mara stared at the clock on her bench. The washer was still there, but a later repairer had shortened the pendulum to compensate again. Two corrections were fighting each other. She restored the pendulum to its proper length and removed the washer. By morning, the clock had kept perfect time.

Mara did not abandon her tablet. Instead, she photographed every ledger page and linked the images to her database. The sketches resisted easy translation: Tomas had drawn pressure, direction, and proportion with lines that were economical but not quite standardized. Mara began adding her own diagrams, first on the tablet and then, when a shape needed the quick judgment of her wrist, in the remaining pages of the ledger.

Months later, an apprentice asked why she bothered with a book that could not be backed up or sorted. Mara said the ledger did not replace the database. It recorded a kind of attention the database had not yet learned to ask for. She turned to a blank page, dated it, and drew the peculiar bend in a lamp’s switch.

Mara later created a database field called “reason for choice,” but she did not require a paragraph for every repair. Sometimes the reason was already visible in a photograph; sometimes three quick lines showed it better. The field merely reminded a repairer that a changed part was not the whole story. Why that part had been changed could matter years later.

She also invited Tomas to the shop one afternoon. He laughed at several of his old sketches and could not remember making them. Yet when Mara showed him the lamp switch, he asked why she had drawn the bend from above instead of from the side. She turned the page and tried again. The ledger’s value, she realized, did not come from age or from Tomas’s authority. It came from a habit of making attention visible enough for another person to question. Her new drawing kept both views.

The shop’s customers noticed the change slowly. Invoices now included a small diagram when a repair depended on an unusual alignment or substituted part. Most customers ignored the image, but a few asked for copies. One brought back a fan after moving apartments and pointed to the earlier diagram; the new vibration, she said, began only after the move. Mara used the drawing to rule out two possible causes before opening the housing. The ledger had become neither relic nor master record. It was one layer in a system designed to preserve decisions that otherwise disappeared when a repaired object left the bench.

READING PASSAGE 3: Two Views of Pocket Parks
PASSAGE A
A pocket park occupies only a small lot, sometimes the footprint of a single demolished building. Its scale is often treated as a weakness: a few benches and trees cannot provide a playing field or a long walking path. Yet scale can also be the park’s advantage. Because a pocket park is inserted directly into a block, it can place shade, seating, and plant life within a short walk of residents who may not reach a large park often.

Designers should begin with repeated observation. A beautiful plan may fail if it ignores the hour when an adjacent restaurant needs deliveries or the path students take after school. Movable chairs, durable planting beds, and one clear open area can support several uses without pretending that the lot is larger than it is. Success should be measured locally: Are people staying longer on the block? Do older residents have a comfortable place to rest? Does rain soak into soil instead of rushing into a drain?

PASSAGE B
The enthusiasm for pocket parks sometimes outruns the evidence used to justify them. A photograph of a crowded opening day says little about use six months later. A city may celebrate a tiny new park while postponing maintenance at larger parks that serve far more people. Small sites also create a tempting illusion of low cost. The land may be donated, but irrigation, trash collection, lighting, and repairs continue every year.

This does not mean that small parks are a mistake. It means that cities should compare them with other investments. A shaded bus stop, a safer crossing, or grants for existing courtyards may offer more benefit on some blocks. Before choosing a pocket park, planners should state the problem they intend to solve and collect evidence after the ribbon is cut. A site that remains useful deserves support; one that does not should teach the city to choose differently next time.

Passage B also cautions against choosing measures only after a project opens. If planners celebrate whichever number improves, almost any site can be called successful. A stronger evaluation names a few outcomes in advance, records conditions before construction, and checks whether benefits persist across seasons. Those steps need not turn a small park into a research laboratory. They simply connect public claims to observations that residents and officials can examine.

Under that standard, the local questions favored by Passage A become especially useful. Shade, rest, drainage, and time spent on the block can all be observed at a scale appropriate to the site. The disagreement is therefore less about whether small parks can help than about what should happen before a city assumes that one will.

Both approaches also imply that maintenance belongs in the original design. Passage A’s movable chairs and planting beds remain advantages only if someone repairs, waters, and rearranges them. Passage B’s comparison of annual costs asks planners to identify that responsibility before construction. A neglected lot painted green for an opening ceremony would satisfy neither writer. For both, the physical size of the site is less decisive than the fit between a defined local need, an adaptable design, and evidence collected over enough time to show whether the space continues to serve people after its novelty fades.

Residents can contribute to that evidence without being reduced to a single satisfaction score. Short interviews may reveal why a bench remains empty, while timed observations show whether the report describes an occasional problem or a recurring one. A drainage test can complement both. Passage A would use such information to adapt the site; Passage B would also use it to judge whether continued spending on the site is preferable to another intervention. In each case, observation links a small physical space to the particular public purposes claimed for it.

READING PASSAGE 3: Two Views of Pocket Parks
PASSAGE A
A pocket park occupies only a small lot, sometimes the footprint of a single demolished building. Its scale is often treated as a weakness: a few benches and trees cannot provide a playing field or a long walking path. Yet scale can also be the park’s advantage. Because a pocket park is inserted directly into a block, it can place shade, seating, and plant life within a short walk of residents who may not reach a large park often.

Designers should begin with repeated observation. A beautiful plan may fail if it ignores the hour when an adjacent restaurant needs deliveries or the path students take after school. Movable chairs, durable planting beds, and one clear open area can support several uses without pretending that the lot is larger than it is. Success should be measured locally: Are people staying longer on the block? Do older residents have a comfortable place to rest? Does rain soak into soil instead of rushing into a drain?

PASSAGE B
The enthusiasm for pocket parks sometimes outruns the evidence used to justify them. A photograph of a crowded opening day says little about use six months later. A city may celebrate a tiny new park while postponing maintenance at larger parks that serve far more people. Small sites also create a tempting illusion of low cost. The land may be donated, but irrigation, trash collection, lighting, and repairs continue every year.

This does not mean that small parks are a mistake. It means that cities should compare them with other investments. A shaded bus stop, a safer crossing, or grants for existing courtyards may offer more benefit on some blocks. Before choosing a pocket park, planners should state the problem they intend to solve and collect evidence after the ribbon is cut. A site that remains useful deserves support; one that does not should teach the city to choose differently next time.

Passage B also cautions against choosing measures only after a project opens. If planners celebrate whichever number improves, almost any site can be called successful. A stronger evaluation names a few outcomes in advance, records conditions before construction, and checks whether benefits persist across seasons. Those steps need not turn a small park into a research laboratory. They simply connect public claims to observations that residents and officials can examine.

Under that standard, the local questions favored by Passage A become especially useful. Shade, rest, drainage, and time spent on the block can all be observed at a scale appropriate to the site. The disagreement is therefore less about whether small parks can help than about what should happen before a city assumes that one will.

Both approaches also imply that maintenance belongs in the original design. Passage A’s movable chairs and planting beds remain advantages only if someone repairs, waters, and rearranges them. Passage B’s comparison of annual costs asks planners to identify that responsibility before construction. A neglected lot painted green for an opening ceremony would satisfy neither writer. For both, the physical size of the site is less decisive than the fit between a defined local need, an adaptable design, and evidence collected over enough time to show whether the space continues to serve people after its novelty fades.

Residents can contribute to that evidence without being reduced to a single satisfaction score. Short interviews may reveal why a bench remains empty, while timed observations show whether the report describes an occasional problem or a recurring one. A drainage test can complement both. Passage A would use such information to adapt the site; Passage B would also use it to judge whether continued spending on the site is preferable to another intervention. In each case, observation links a small physical space to the particular public purposes claimed for it.

stimulusMaterial.body:
READING PASSAGE 4: Night Trains and City Heat
A city rail agency testing nighttime service noticed a pattern in electricity use. Trains consumed slightly more energy on the hottest nights, even when passenger counts were similar. Engineers first suspected the air-conditioning systems inside the cars. Measurements showed that those systems mattered, but they did not explain the entire increase.

Rails absorb heat during the day and release it slowly after sunset. On warmer rails, electrical resistance rises slightly, and some trackside equipment requires more cooling. The effect for one train is small. Across hundreds of trips, however, small increases accumulate. The agency compared average energy per trip with the temperature measured at 10:00 p.m. for six test nights. The accompanying graph shows the results.

The data reveal an association, not a complete explanation. The hottest nights may also have different passenger patterns, delays, or wind conditions. To isolate the role of temperature, the agency plans to compare trains of the same model traveling the same route and stopping pattern. Engineers will also place sensors at shaded and unshaded track sections because air temperature alone may not represent rail temperature.

Even before that study is complete, the result can guide operations. Trains can be pre-cooled in the depot, where cooling equipment is more efficient, and nonessential trackside cabinets can be shaded. Neither step is expected to transform the system’s energy budget. The value lies in identifying several modest improvements that do not reduce service.

The next test will run for eight weeks rather than six selected nights. Each train will report energy used by propulsion, cabin cooling, and auxiliary systems separately. Track sensors will record rail temperature every five minutes, and dispatch records will identify delays. If energy remains associated with rail temperature after those factors are considered, the engineers will have a stronger basis for estimating the trackside contribution.

A different result would still be useful. If cabin cooling explains nearly all of the increase, the agency could focus on depot procedures rather than track equipment. In either case, the six-night graph has served its purpose: it has identified a pattern precise enough to investigate, but not precise enough to treat as a settled cause.

The agency will publish the follow-up data by trip rather than only as nightly averages. That choice will let analysts test whether a handful of delayed trains account for much of the increase. It will also reveal whether pre-cooling changes energy use at the depot, during the trip, or both. Riders are unlikely to notice any of these measurements, and that is part of the goal: the proposed adjustments preserve the same timetable and cabin comfort. The study treats efficiency as an accumulation of small operational choices, each supported by a pattern that survives a fair comparison.

Engineers will also compare nights with similar temperatures but different humidity and wind. Those variables can change how hard cooling equipment works and how quickly rails release stored heat. A result that weakens after these comparisons would not make the original graph erroneous; it would show that temperature had been standing in for a more complicated set of conditions. The follow-up study is designed precisely to discover whether the simple relationship remains useful after the hidden differences between nights are made visible.

stimulusMaterial.title: Night Trains and City Heat
stimulusMaterial.body:
READING PASSAGE 4: Night Trains and City Heat
A city rail agency testing nighttime service noticed a pattern in electricity use. Trains consumed slightly more energy on the hottest nights, even when passenger counts were similar. Engineers first suspected the air-conditioning systems inside the cars. Measurements showed that those systems mattered, but they did not explain the entire increase.

Rails absorb heat during the day and release it slowly after sunset. On warmer rails, electrical resistance rises slightly, and some trackside equipment requires more cooling. The effect for one train is small. Across hundreds of trips, however, small increases accumulate. The agency compared average energy per trip with the temperature measured at 10:00 p.m. for six test nights. The accompanying graph shows the results.

The data reveal an association, not a complete explanation. The hottest nights may also have different passenger patterns, delays, or wind conditions. To isolate the role of temperature, the agency plans to compare trains of the same model traveling the same route and stopping pattern. Engineers will also place sensors at shaded and unshaded track sections because air temperature alone may not represent rail temperature.

Even before that study is complete, the result can guide operations. Trains can be pre-cooled in the depot, where cooling equipment is more efficient, and nonessential trackside cabinets can be shaded. Neither step is expected to transform the system’s energy budget. The value lies in identifying several modest improvements that do not reduce service.

The next test will run for eight weeks rather than six selected nights. Each train will report energy used by propulsion, cabin cooling, and auxiliary systems separately. Track sensors will record rail temperature every five minutes, and dispatch records will identify delays. If energy remains associated with rail temperature after those factors are considered, the engineers will have a stronger basis for estimating the trackside contribution.

A different result would still be useful. If cabin cooling explains nearly all of the increase, the agency could focus on depot procedures rather than track equipment. In either case, the six-night graph has served its purpose: it has identified a pattern precise enough to investigate, but not precise enough to treat as a settled cause.

The agency will publish the follow-up data by trip rather than only as nightly averages. That choice will let analysts test whether a handful of delayed trains account for much of the increase. It will also reveal whether pre-cooling changes energy use at the depot, during the trip, or both. Riders are unlikely to notice any of these measurements, and that is part of the goal: the proposed adjustments preserve the same timetable and cabin comfort. The study treats efficiency as an accumulation of small operational choices, each supported by a pattern that survives a fair comparison.

Engineers will also compare nights with similar temperatures but different humidity and wind. Those variables can change how hard cooling equipment works and how quickly rails release stored heat. A result that weakens after these comparisons would not make the original graph erroneous; it would show that temperature had been standing in for a more complicated set of conditions. The follow-up study is designed precisely to discover whether the simple relationship remains useful after the hidden differences between nights are made visible.

stimulusMaterial.body:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 6: Origins of Bright Crater Rays
Three students discuss why some young impact craters have bright rays extending across the surface.

Student 1: The rays consist mainly of fresh material excavated from beneath a dark, weathered surface. With time, exposure to radiation and tiny impacts darkens the rays until they resemble the surrounding ground.

Student 2: The material is not intrinsically brighter. Impact fragments roughen the surface, and the rough texture reflects sunlight toward the observer at certain angles. As small grains settle, the directional reflection weakens.

Student 3: Both excavation and texture matter. Fresh subsurface material begins brighter than the surface, and rough fragment deposits enhance that contrast. Weathering and settling therefore work together to fade the rays.

questions.teachingTopic: Conflicting Viewpoints — Earth and Space Science
questions.stem: Which prediction is most consistent with Student 3?

options.A: Changing either relevant factor could never affect the observation.
options.B: Student 3 would predict that both weathering of grains and smoothing of the deposit reduce ray brightness.
options.C: Only a factor that no student mentions could matter.
options.D: The phenomenon should remain perfectly constant over unlimited time.

questions.explanation: The prediction follows from Student 3’s combined-mechanism explanation.

stimulusMaterial.title: Battery Voltage at Different Temperatures
stimulusMaterial.body:
SCIENCE PASSAGE 7: Battery Voltage at Different Temperatures
Students placed identical batteries in temperature-controlled chambers for 30 minutes. They then connected each battery to the same resistor and recorded voltage immediately and after 5 minutes. Each temperature condition used a new battery from the same package.
